course.title: Distributivity and the cross terms in a square
course.sourceAnchor: AoPS Introduction to Algebra2007, sections1.4 and11.1; catalogue095fa482 rows11,679,680; owner outline LS2
course.rightsAnchor: Original paraphrased instructional activities with source/page metadata. Textbook bytes are excluded; third-party rights and repository license remain separate and unresolved.

nodes.title: Prepare by counting the same rectangle twice
nodes.body: Draw a rectangle with four rows and a vertical split into widths two and three. Count cells by combining widths, then by combining the two smaller rectangles. Explain why both counts agree.
nodes.exampleText: 4*(2+3)=4*2+4*3. Name the common factor and the two summands.
nodes.hint: Keep the number of rows fixed while splitting the width.

nodes.title: Account for every product in a square
nodes.body: Write a square as a product of two identical sums. Each first-factor term multiplies each second-factor term. Combine the two equal cross products only after writing both.
nodes.worked: (t+3)*(t+3)=t*t+t*3+3*t+3*3=t*t+6*t+9. The two cross products have different positions in the product table.
nodes.hint: Use a two by two table with t and 3 on both sides.

nodes.title: Reconstruct what the identity means
nodes.body: A binomial has two terms. An identity states an equality throughout a specified domain. Reconstruct these meanings and explain why a few matching substitutions do not provide the requested symbolic justification.
nodes.exercise: Define a binomial square identity over Q and describe the quantifier in your own words.
nodes.hint: Separate the names of the expressions from the claim that relates them for every input.

nodes.title: Submit the exact coefficients
nodes.body: Apply the four-product argument to the installed goal (x+1)*(x+1) over Q[x]. Enter constant, linear and quadratic coefficients. The exact checker supports this fixed goal, including invalid alternatives.
nodes.hint: Write all four products; compare how many contribute a term of degree one.

nodes.title: Find the missing cross products
nodes.body: A proposed argument says that squaring u+v gives u*u+v*v because each term can be squared separately. Identify the unjustified step and use u=2,v=1 to refute the proposed identity.
nodes.exercise: Give the two missing products and a counterexample. Distinguish refutation from proof of the correct general formula.
nodes.hint: Compare the proposal with the full product table before substituting numbers.

nodes.title: Independent proof of a special case
nodes.body: Work without hints. Prove the stated identity for every natural number x using distributivity. A checked reference theorem is available to the course reviewer; your handwritten argument still needs teacher review.
nodes.exercise: For every x in Nat, prove (x+1)*(x+1)=x*x+2*x+1. State the domain and justify each equality.

nodes.title: Transfer from expansion to recognition
nodes.body: Reverse the reasoning: consider y*y+14*y+49. Recognize a square of a binomial and justify the middle term. Then explain what changes if 14*y is replaced by 12*y. This goal requires teacher review.
nodes.exercise: Factor y*y+14*y+49 and explain why changing only the middle coefficient can destroy the square pattern.
nodes.hint: A candidate square must account for its first, middle and final terms together.

nodes.title: Later reconstruction and error diagnosis
nodes.body: After the scheduled delay, reconstruct the binomial-square argument with no hint. Explain why the cross term is doubled and diagnose the dropped-term argument with a fresh counterexample.
nodes.review: Seven-day authored review policy. This schedule records due work, not measured retention. Keep the original course, policy, source and assistance references.

Account for both cross products in a binomial square
Distinguish identity, counterexample, exact coefficient evidence and informal proof
Recognize a square from all three coefficients and revisit reasoning after a delay
notationGuide: Q[x] is the routine exact coefficient-checker domain
Nat is the domain of the checked reference specialization
A universal identity is not established by trying a few values
